It was addressed to a man or woman -- I don't know whether it's man or woman -- Cees Hendriks. The subject was questioning with German and Austrian authorities concerning the arrest of Delalic and Mucic. Does that refresh your memory at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really in terms of detail, but it's quite possible I might have informed Mr. Cees Hendriks of how things were going in terms of the procedure and investigation, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cees Hendriks was the person you were dealing with in Vienna; is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all. I think there's a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have sent that -- were you sending memoranda in English, French or German?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends. Both languages, English and French, are official of the Tribunal, so I could use either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at the German and see if you recognise this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May the Prosecution see that first, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course. I hope my learned friend's German is as good as mine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't speak any German at all, so it's a bit difficult for me to tell you what this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just have a look, please, at the second page, Mr. Abribat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there is a paragraph at the end which is ten lines long which happens the word "Osterreich" in it. Do you see that, about eight or ten lines up from the bottom? . Would it assist you if I show you where I am referring to, Mr. Abribat? I do not want to be unfair to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please, if you would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would your Honours excuse me for a moment? (Indicating). Now appreciating that you do not read German, what I suggest to you is contained in there, and this is an approximate translation: "After the arrest there are possibilities for the handover of the arrested persons: 1: Opening of the legal proceedings under Austrian law by the Austrian authorities. (The law should be passed). After they enact the law, the Tribunal should make a request for the handing over of the arrested persons. 2: At a request or with the approval of the of the accused, he could choose to be handed over to the Tribunal instead of Bosnia. If he decides to make this choice, would the Austrian government hand him over to the Tribunal? Concerning that the death penalty exists in Bosnia, this alternative should be more practical and efficient". I suggest to you that you were well before arriving in Vienna to see this man already contemplating the idea that he would be extradited to the Tribunal, Mr. Abribat. That is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I've already told you, yes, I did hope that he would be transferred here. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when he was talking to the court about having a lawyer concerning extradition, that covered being extradited to The Hague, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't really say, because the extradition procedure, I don't know whether it was for the extradition by the Tribunal or to another country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Abribat, you knew full well at the end of the interview with Judge Peter Sada, which completed itself at 3.10, you knew, didn't you, that Mr. Mucic wanted to have a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that, I suggest, came as a blow to you, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, and I don't really see why you're insisting on that part, because I told you that there was the matter of whether there was going to be a lawyer there or not. I didn't get a full translation. I was told that it was in connection with the extradition procedure and that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that an indictment was already almost complete and all the material to support it had been gathered together? Did you know that, who you were in charge of this investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An indictment by the International Tribunal, do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Abribat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the indictment I don't know where it stood when we were in Vienna. I don't recall. But I did hope there would be an indictment, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it is a matter of public record that it was 21st March 1996, Mr. Abribat, three days after you went to Vienna to go and have a chat with Mr. Mucic. Are you saying to us that you didn't know that that was about to be placed before His Honour Judge Jorda, you who set up this investigation and were in charge of it? You did not know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the dates you mentioned, no, but you say a chat. Well, I don't agree to the use of that term, a chat. We are talking about something that was quite in accordance with the rules and the procedures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying you did not know that an indictment was about to be placed before Judge Jorda? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that an indictment was being prepared and what I've told you is that I didn't know exactly where it stood, and what the dates at which it was submitted or finalised and brought before Judge Jorda, no, I didn't know what those dates were, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in a terrible hurry to interview this man, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I've never had that kind of an attitude in investigations. I go ahead with the investigations at the right speed, taking the right precautions and abiding by the procedures. It is the procedures which dictate the speed at which you proceed, not how fast you want to go yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest you knew full well there was an indictment about to be placed before the court for confirmation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I knew that an indictment was being prepared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wanted to complete interviewing this man before he got back to The Hague, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. You are misinterpreting things there, because I left Vienna before the questioning was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you wanted to question him and complete that process before he got back to The Hague in order to take advantage of the confusion of his being arrested, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I do not know where you get these kind of illusions from. Those are just -- I don't work on that basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, what I suggest happened was that you became angry before the court hearing before Judge Sada and the knowledge that you -- that he wanted to have a lawyer; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I wasn't angered at all. Quite frankly I don't understand the point of your questions. You make these illusions, you make these statements, but that's not it at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then conducted a short, 20 minute conversation with the defendant after seeing Dr. Sada?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of which you told Mr. Mucic that he could go home at the end of questioning if you talked to him without a lawyer; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's absolutely wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But made it plain to him if he wanted to hang on with a lawyer that he was going to be there forever and kept locked up; is that not it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know which country you come from and what rules you have, but in my country that's not how it works. We have rules of procedure. We have texts and we stick to the texts. So what you're saying is absolutely untrue. I saw Mr. Mucic on two occasions, as I've already explained. The first time it was on the 18th for two or three minutes simply to explain to him the stages of the procedure and the second time it was on the 19th to go ahead with the interview, but I strictly abided by the letter and the spirit of the texts I was bound to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke to Mr. Mucic with the cameras rolling for the first time, Mr. Abribat you said this, amongst other things: "The first question is: do you agree to answer our questions without the presence of an attorney in accordance with our previous conversation". Which previous conversation are you referring to there, Mr. Abribat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I thought I explained that this morning, that I was referring to the two or three minutes conversation I had with Mr. Mucic on the 18th, that is to say when I told him what the procedures of the Tribunal were and I referred back to that so that there would be no problem in that. I'd seen Mr. Mucic for three minutes on the 18th, so I stated that I had seen him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That, I suggest, was in the 20 minutes -- that conversation was in the 20 minutes between Dr. Sada seeing him and you starting the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I am sticking to what I said. That is not true. I never saw Mr. Mucic for any 20 minutes. That's absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did that because you were determined that he should be interviewed somehow or another without a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Listen, sir, I think you have certain desires. You'd like things to be what they're not. I've been involved in questioning for 20 years. I always prepare my questions and I had prepared things for Mr. Mucic. Maybe I could find my notes, my preparatory material. In that material I have a reference to the presence of an attorney. If I might just add something, your Honours. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: If it is answered with reference to the questions put to you, if it has any relevance to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, and you'll judge for yourselves. It's not for me to say. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you can?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply before going on an assignment -- before going to Vienna in connection with the arrest of Mucic we asked for a list of the lawyers available on call in Vienna so that we don't have to waste time if Mr. Mucic decided that he did want a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you gave evidence this morning, you told us concerning what happened before the cameras began and you said this: "This is the equipment we're going to use in order to record this hearing. I'm also going to show you the video recorder saying this is the other piece of equipment that I'm going to use and we will respect the forms that I gave to you yesterday." What forms did you give to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Meaning that I'll follow the Rules of Procedure that were in effect at the Tribunal for the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by the word "forms" Mr. Abribat? Are you talking about some document that you gave to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, when I talk about these -- by this term I mean the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you mean, in fact, is the word "formalities", not "forms"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how it was interpreted into English or what the interpretation would be, but yes, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Abribat, just let me make it absolutely plain once again what I'm suggesting to you. You, during the course of the 20 minutes said things to Mr. Mucic designed to persuade him to do without a lawyer, a lawyer you knew he wanted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I too will be very clear. Why do you refer to this 20 minutes that I'm not even aware of? What allows you to assert that I had a private 20 minute discussion with Mucic? I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us this morning this, when you were asked by Ms. McHenry -- you were asked this question: "Among the rights that you advised Mr. Mucic of, did you advise him that he had the right to an attorney and if he had not had the possibility of getting one himself, one would be assigned to him". Your reply was this: "Yes, absolutely. I said it twice before we began the questions"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said it twice. I said it on the 18th when I saw him for the first time, and on the 19th, when we began the interview. That's the two times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You go on in the course of your evidence: "It was the same thing under the circumstances." I'm sorry. That is not a good point. I do apologise. I suggest what you meant there was you had had a conversation with him prior to commencing the formal part of the questions under Rule 43?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had no conversation with Mr. Mucic. I can tell you for the nth time that I saw him for two minutes on the 18th with the translator and the Austrian police officer, and then I saw Mucic for the interview after having been with the judge in his office a little while the judge explained to me what Mucic's status was. I never saw him outside those two very specific occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Immediately before the luncheon adjournment you were asked this question: "Question: Did you make any reference to the fact that he'd previously spoken, albeit briefly, with Mr. Mucic in the recorded part of the interview? Answer: Yes, of course. I referred to that because for me I simply had to refer to the first explanation of his rights. That would seem normal to me for us to speak what has been said. I said: "I have already explained your rights to you. I'm going to repeat what I've said and afterwards you will give your answer and say whether or not you agree to speak". When did you have that conversation with the defendant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you ask that question again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Abribat. You gave evidence this morning in the following terms. The question was asked of you in this way: "Question: did you make any reference to the fact that he had previously spoken, albeit briefly, with Mr. Mucic in the recorded part of the interview? Answer: Yes, of course. I referred to that because for me I simply had to refer to the first explanation of his rights. That would seem normal to me for us to speak what has been said. I said: "I have already explained your rights to you. I'm going to repeat what I've said and afterwards you will give your answer and say whether you agree or not". When do you say that that conversation I've just read out took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said this morning is that before the recording began I saw Mr. Mucic and I said to him that: "We're going to begin the recording of the interview if you agree that this be done without a lawyer and we'll begin by reading your rights". Then I began the recording by reading out the rights. The first sentence of the interview I believe that we are this or that place before this or that person, that we're in the presence of Mr. Mucic and then I think that I have to ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Abribat, that conversation that you related to us this morning, that's not recorded in the interview, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That isn't a conversation. That's simply setting up the process to be used -- the procedure to be used for the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, I suggest that you did -- that's an indication that you did have a conversation about having a lawyer with him before the cameras started to roll and that you're not telling the truth to this Tribunal about that, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think that you are making an incorrect interpretation. You're playing with words. I'm telling you the exact truth, the exact truth to this Tribunal, that I never attempted to take away any of the Mucic's rights or betray the spirit of the Rules of Evidence and Procedure. Perhaps in your country that is the way people work, but not in mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that despite what you said this morning that you had had this conversation, you are now saying you did not have this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that you're playing with words. I did not have a conversation. I simply explained to Mr. Mucic and this is what you're trying to show, that when explains things too much, it could be a mistake. So contrary to what you might think I took my time to explain it but I didn't have a conversation at all. As far as the second time was concerned, I was with Mr. Mucic. I recorded the interview and I simply said that: "We are now going to ask you questions according to the formalities that are in effect at the Tribunal, that is we are going to record what we're going to do" and I showed him the equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present during each of the interviews that was conducted by the OTP with Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was only there on the 19th. After that I came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the interview on 19th March was there any particular reason why you did not set out in that interview that he was a suspect in a war crimes matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't really understand the sense of your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it is quite simple, Mr. Abribat. In that interview you did not say to him in terms: "You are a suspect in connection with war crimes committed at the Celebici camp between May 1992 and November 1992", did you? You never said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, will you accept from me that it isn't there, Mr. Abribat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why could I agree with what you're saying? I'm just saying I don't remember. However, what I do remember is that it was clearly pointed out to Mr. Mucic for what reasons the international Tribunal wished to meet him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't do that at the beginning of the formal interview with him, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. We'd have to listen to the recording.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we've got the transcript, Mr. Abribat. Will you accept from me or not that it isn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what has to be accepted or not from you. I really do not know. You said a little while ago that I had spoken for 20 minutes with Mr. Mucic. You assert this in a way in my opinion which is completely false. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the conclusion of the interviewing that you carried out why didn't you offer him an opportunity to clarify anything he had said or to add anything that he wished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The questions were interrupted. The guards of the prison interrupted us and said that things were over, that their shift was over and we had to stop. I asked" could we go on?" They said "no, that's it". Therefore, we stopped the questioning, but I can tell you it was not complete, because the next day it was taken up again, it was resumed and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was nothing to prevent you complying with Rule 43(3), was there, at the end of that interview, Mr. Abribat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interview was not complete and I didn't want to say anything further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me, Mr. Abribat. The interview came to an end, didn't it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. I think this is arguing with the witness. The witness has been very patient. The transcript speaks and I think he has answered this question very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: With great respect, I don't think he has answered the question at all clearly. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: He can answer it again. It's a simple question. It's quite simple. You can answer it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is that the interview had been interrupted by the guards. Is that what you are asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It is quite simple, Mr. Abribat. Did the interview come to an end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interview was interrupted by the guards. They told us to stop at a specific point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying that it didn't come to a conclusion. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm telling you it was finished because we had been interrupted by the guards but that the questioning resumed the next day with another investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the fact that it was merely interrupted rather than concluded, that is a justification for you not to ask him whether he wishes to clarify anything; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't even ask that question because we were stopped by the guard. They took him away because their shift was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. No further questions. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You also want to ask questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I thought Mr. Greaves was asking them on behalf of --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Well, you can do so if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves carried out the cross-examination on behalf of the defence, but I would like to join in this cross-examination of Mr. Abribat. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry, counsel. May I be heard just for one minute? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution does object. The judges made it very clear in the beginning that one counsel would be expected to ask. There are, I believe, ten defence counsel appointed to represent the accused, and I think it would be unfair to witnesses in general. If it's just one or two questions for this witness, we will not particularly stand on this objection, but the Prosecution does object to multiple counsel for the same accused asking -- cross-examining the witnesses. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually one is getting a little fed up with the difference of professional practice being demonstrated here. I thought if Mr. Greaves has gone into such details in asking questions, cross-examining, at least he had the leave of lead counsel to do so. I did not expect lead counsel to get up to ask questions again over and above whatever has been done. I think you should understand what professional practice looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand, but your Honours have already allowed me to put my questions and it was after that that my learned colleague from the Prosecution objected, so I think that I have been given the opportunity to cross-examine the witness but, of course, it is up to you to rule on this, whether I may begin the cross-examination, but let me repeat: you allowed me to speak and only then did the representative of the Prosecution object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not sure two counsel for the same accused unless it is stated right at the beginning of the cross-examination can be allowed to cross-examine the same witness. Mr. Greaves has done that. He should have told us that he is going to cross-examine on certain aspects and the lead counsel will cross-examine on the other aspects. This is just not done. You cannot have two cross-examinations going on like this. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Obviously there is no consultation between you and your co-counsel. I have observed that not only in this instance. You will try and consult properly with co-counsel so that you know how to organise the defence of your client. This is not the first instance. That is why it is giving one a little problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That can come to harrassing a witness. You are covering the same ground all over again. Mr. Greaves could have told us right at the beginning he is cross-examining with regard to this aspect of the evidence and the lead counsel will do it with the other aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I respect your position and I will withdraw my questions, but the questions that I wished to put to Mr. Abribat will be possible for me to put to the next witness when I shall take advantage of that right that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I have a question to ask from the witness. While you were explaining the rights to the suspect that he did not have to make a statement, he had a right to counsel and he had to -- he could remain silent if he wanted, and if he made a statement that it was used in evidence against him, was it also video recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 18th, when I explained the rules of procedure -- no, of course not. It was not recorded. I explained to him merely what the stages were, and then on the 19th when we began the interview I repeated his rights to him and his rights were recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why was that not video recorded? That would have ended some of the controversy which is being raised before us. You were questioning him whether you want a counsel, whether you want to remain silent, whether you know that this evidence will be used in evidence before you. Why was that not video recorded if you were questioning him within the meaning of Rule 43?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was recorded during the interview on the 19th. Everything was recorded on the 19th including the rights according to rules 42 and 43. The difference that I was making was on the 18th I explained it to him, because I explained that in order to record he had to authorise my doing so. So first I printed things to him and at the time that the interview took place, that is on the 19th, it was recorded, including the rights, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, counsel for Mr. Delalic does have questions for this witness, but given the time I am not sure whether you want to start now or perhaps take the break. Whatever you feel is best. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The break is at 4 o'clock. We can break at 4 o'clock and come back. Cross-examination by Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: May it please the courts ... JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I have a few questions for you as well. Could you remind us when you joined the office of the OTP as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was recruited by the Tribunal in March or April of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave the office of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: January 1, 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were the person responsible for investigation in the Celebici case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you become responsible for investigations in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the beginning when I was sent to the Tribunal I was sent to be the head of the investigating team. That is from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was all or only a part of your time spent investigating Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I devoted a lot of time to investigating Celebici, but that was not the only investigation that we had begun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many other cases were you working on?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to other questions about other investigations. I think that the matter of what is going on in the Prosecutor's Office with respect to other investigations, including how many investigations this particular team was working on, are improper and irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can ask this question. I just wonder what percentage of his time -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You can ask your questions. I do not see any relevance in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Aside from Celebici how many other cases were you investigating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were carrying out investigations in two other areas, two other directions as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how much of your time would you say in percentage, if you will, was spent on Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Percentage of time depended on the organisation of our work. When we were working on Celebici we did it 100 per cent, and when we were working on other investigations, we did the same thing for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in the Office of the Prosecution for how long? A year and a half; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little longer than that. 21 months, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of those 21 months, how many were spent on Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The entire first year and I would say about -- so I would say about fifteen months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fifteen months, 100 per cent of your time was spent investigating Celebici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I worked for fifteen months but I am talking about the first fifteen months of my work within the Tribunal. During the first fifteen months I also looked at other possibilities which might lead to investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly while you were working on Celebici for fifteen months, that's the only case you were investigating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't express myself right, the first fifteen months were devoted to the Celebici investigation. The team worked on the Celebici camp, but during the first fifteen months I also had occasion to work in other areas of investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were the head of a team. Is that the proper way to explain your role in investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was responsible for the investigating team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in the team that investigated Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to questions about how the Office of the Prosecutor is organised and set up. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Why do you object to how the particular investigation was organised?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Because I think matters of how the Office of the Prosecutor is set up and conducts its investigations are privileged, and it's -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: There is no such privilege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What privilege are you claiming?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: With respect to the internal workings of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are talking about privilege now so I would like to know what is the basis of your claiming privilege.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Maybe I expressed myself badly with respect to privilege, but I don't believe that questions about exactly how the Office of the Prosecutor is organised and conducts its investigation are proper. I believe they are irrelevant. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: There might be questions leading us to how far he could have effectively have done some of the things he stated he has done, so let him answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I will repeat my question to him, sir. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In your team how many people worked under you while investigating Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It fluctuated. I could say about 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all 12 of these people reported back to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the backgrounds of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The professional training or background of those people really went into three areas. They were professional investigators. Most of them come from police services. There were also legal specialists. Then there were analysts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these three categories, you say they all reported back to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "analysts"? What kind of people are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The analysts are people who are responsible for studying and synthesising all the documents and anything which may have to do with the conflict which took place in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Typically what would their background be? The first two categories was police and second legal. What would the analysts' background be typically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you what the traditional analyst's background is, but I can tell you these people who were specialists in studying documents somewhat like a historian or a journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself work directly out of an office of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did you spend most of your time in the office or in the field yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hadn't really calculated the exact percentages, but I can say that I was on many assignments in Bosnia, about fifteen or 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fifteen or 20 dealing with Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Object as to relevance. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: More than fifteen for 20 times in the field? That's what you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I travelled to Bosnia between fifteen and 20 times, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Of those fifteen or 20 times how many times were you there investigating as to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection as to relevancy. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Why don't you leave him to answer the question? Please kindly answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About ten missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: As you know, there are four co-accused in this case. Did the members of your team investigate all four of the co-accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not quite what the methodology was. Within the team we all worked on Celebici, which means that there was not any kind of division between those investigators who were specifically charged with working on one of the accused, but it was a distribution which had to do with the interests of the work. It was not done according to the name or the position of the accused, if that's what your question is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, on what basis was it done, if it's not according to the person's name? How was work divided up in investigating among the four accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The investigating work is work which I think of as typical police work. Therefore there is a police investigation which takes place in four stages. First of all, one must establish the facts. After that, one must find witnesses and victims. Then one must collect evidence, and the last stage is arresting people and bringing them before the court. So depending on the organisation of these four steps you organise your work and the first work which had to do with analysing the facts, this was the work which everybody worked on, but specifically the analysts. We evaluated the facts and then we sought out the victims and witnesses, which took us the most time, and this is why for this case we went to Bosnia about ten times in order to try to find people. After the end of the missions we were in a position to meet many of the victims and the witnesses and after that we tried to collect as much evidence as possible in order to implicate people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Through your investigations I'm sure you learned about the military structures in Bosnia-Herzegovina as they existed in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of these military structures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military structure at that time, the beginning of the war, that is through 1992 it evolved, because Bosnia was not prepared for this type of conflict and they were attempting to try to find a traditional military structure, as would be found in countries with their own military institutions. Therefore what had to be done at that time was to try to understand what the situation of the forces were. They had to set up a military hierarchy and an organisation. There was an organisation, but it evolved as the conflict went on and was constantly being changed and it was never set up in a traditional sense as it would be found in another place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In early 1992 did you know the names of the military structures in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask for the relevance -- well, may I object without any kind of showing of relevance. This witness has not been established as an expert in military structures and I don't see the relevance for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Well, he is the head of the investigating team, so they can ask him questions maybe not relevant entirely to the evidence which he gave in direct examination but he is the head of the investigating agency. Therefore they probably want to find something from him which he learned as head, because everyone is reporting to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Shall I repeat my question for you? We are talking about the names of the military structures and I'm asking you: do you know the names of the military structures in Bosnia in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The structure of the Bosnian Army around 1992 was what was known as the Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence was an old structure that dated from the time of Yugoslavia, which was composed of what one could say, a kind of a people's defence, people who were in their villages or who worked -- or in their workplaces who could be put into a kind of military structure as it existed in the former East Block countries. Therefore, the Bosnian Army was constituted on that basis, and on that basis they tried to set up a military structure which would be divided region by region, which had its own hierarchy and which had to report to the Supreme command at Sarajevo. Additional difficulty at that time is for a great deal of time and throughout 1992 there were no ranks within that military Bosnian structure. It was not an army, as I said, not a traditional army. So one does not have references to specific ranks, but rather to responsibility, functions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of an organisation called MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me MUP was the police service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your investigations show that in early 1992 both MUP and TO were composed of Muslims, Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The three communities were represented within the Bosnian structures, but very quickly there was total control of everything that had to do with giving out orders by the Muslim community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This composition of MUP and TO existed in the Konjic municipality; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far the Muslim and Croatian communities, yes, but not for the Serbian community, as you have alluded to because in that region there was a great preponderance of Croats and Muslims. There were very few Serbs. They were very much in the minority. There were only about two or three villages. More specifically Serbian and the percentage of those cities was really quite low.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do know that in the Konjic municipality there were Muslims, Croats and Serbs who were members of MUP and TO in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: MUP, Territorial Defence. MUP certainly; Territorial Defence, I'm not so sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Through your investigations did you learn about civilian structures in the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The municipality was under the authority, under the war council. I think that's what it was called. They had set up structures which derived from the conflict, from the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your information showed as well that within the civilian structures they were composed of Muslims, Croats and Serbs as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could see those communities, but as far as the Serbians were concerned, they were removed very quickly from any leadership bodies, any representative bodies, in fact. The Croats were set aside a little bit later during 1994. Afterwards the representative organs and the decision-making organs, that is the organs that made the decisions, were under total control of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it this information about military and civilian structures came to you in part from the people in your team who reported to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's part of investigating work, yes, and then there's the analytical work of all the documents that we'd gathered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point did you yourself verify the accuracy of the information you have received from your investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our work consisted, in fact, of verifying as much as could be verified having to do with the initial information and to the extent that could be verified, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be looked at and checked or double checked; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One checks what one can. In so far as one has several -- a delay of several years -- this is not an ordinary criminal investigation. We came to Bosnia in 1995, 1996. That is three -- three or four years had already passed since the time the acts had been committed. What gives strength to an organisation is if one can arrive early, one can congeal, if you like, a situation and then base the direction of your investigation on that. That was not the case in this case. When there is -- where there was a conflict. What was possible for us to check, we did try to check, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question on this point is I assume you yourself collected some of this information personally on military and civilian structures through your trips; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you'd agree with me that it's fair to say that you were familiar with the military structures and organisation in the Konjic municipality in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about that structure. I was not -- I did not have expert knowledge perhaps, but sufficient knowledge, yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Professor O'Sullivan, I think the Trial Chamber will rise now for 30 minutes. (4.00pm) (Short break) (4.30 pm) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can you please invite the witness? (Witness re-entered court) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Please inform Mr. Abribat he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Abribat, may I remind you that you are still under oath. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Sir, before the break you recall that we were discussing your knowledge of the military and political structures in Konjic municipality. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the court that based on investigations that your team had carried out and that you had carried out you knew that there was a TO and MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also told the court that in early 1992 TO and MUP were composed of people from three groups: Muslim, Croat and Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with regard to MUP, yes, but with regard to Territorial Defence I said that I didn't necessarily go along with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying your investigations showed that the TO was not composed of Muslims, Croatians and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in the Konjic region in particular I don't think that there were any Serbs in the Territorial Defence once the conflict started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall on March 14th, 1996 that you prepared a declaration regarding the background in Konjic municipality and Celebici camp in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall the specific date, but if you have the note, then that must be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps with the assistance of the usher we could show this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you recognise this document as your own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you prepared this document yourself on 14th March 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, unless they have done this with the team, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the information contained in this declaration is the result of your investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a summary. It's quite succinct. It's just to outline the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this declaration is based on your knowledge of the situation at that time, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the first page I'm looking at the third full paragraph, the first sentence, which reads: "Beginning in the latter part of May 1992 forces consisting of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats ...". Why did you choose to refer to the forces as Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, knowing that there was a TO and a MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why did I refer to Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats? That's the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Instead of using the correct designation of TO and MUP, which you knew existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but this isn't wrong either. The TO, as I told you earlier on, you had to make things more distinct. You had to talk about the Konjic TO. For example, if you look in Sarajevo, there you would have had Serbs in the TO. So just to make clear here that we are talking about Bosnian Muslims, etc. So I wanted to make that clear. That's why I used these terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we're talking about the Konjic municipality, are we not, in this declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. So to make clear that there were Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats I used those terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO I believe it's an organisation that was made up of Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they exist in the municipality in the latter part of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they existed, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in writing a report for this Tribunal, why did you use terminology which may not correctly reflect military structures in the region of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the contrary, I think I used the right terms. I'm not sure you know just what the HVO is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you if you knew what it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know what the HVO is. The HVO is not a military force in the strict sense. There's also a political side to it. So if you're going to refer to a military structure with the term HVO, you've got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were the author of this report and you chose to use terminology which I put to you is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see what you say is wrong here. When I say it is Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat forces, to make clear there weren't any Bosnian Serbs there, what's wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is incorrect, is it not? That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I fail to see what's wrong. There's forces there made of up of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. I fail to see what's wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I put it to you it is a simplification of a more complex situation. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this war is an extremely complicated matter. Neither you nor I are perhaps sufficiently qualified to sum things up in just a few words and here in this declaration I was trying to be very succinct, so I tried to be as specific as possible referring to the people involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us back up just a second. What did you say the HVO was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That it's an organisation that consisted of the Bosnian Croat population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not correct to say that it's the military wing of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely not. HVO is more than just something military. Now a lot of people have, to simplify, used HVO to refer to the military wing but at the time the HVO had a President who was not a military man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not correct that the HDZ is the civilian branch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there again you've got it wrong. HDZ is the political branch that was representing a part of the Bosnian Croat population and not all the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not correct that the two legal entities at the time in Bosnia were the TO and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know what you mean by legal entities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two constitutionally recognised entities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were among the entities recognised by the constitution, but I think that's also true for the HVO, because there have been some high level negotiations in the Bosnian Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that you're aware of some of the complexities in the situation, yet you chose to simplify for your superiors by using the expression Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a simplification that is wholly consistent with reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't the reality of the situation complex?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this argument between defence counsel and the witness. I think the facts and the different positions have been made very clear and I object to any further discussion. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think it's not necessary pursuing this part of the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. This declaration, your declaration of 14th March 1996, was used in support of the Prosecutor's request for provisional arrest, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the extraordinary measure under Rule 40 of our rules for provisional arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Rule 40 states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, by memory I think this relates to provisional measures taken by the Prosecutor to secure the presence of people who are suspects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the basis on which the Prosecutor relied on Rule 40 in relation to Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he must have referred to the notion of urgency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is there anything in your declaration that suggests that there was a situation of urgency as regards Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The urgency was to prevent any flight or the loss of documentation or pressure that might -- intimidation that might occur, because we want to be sure that we would have sufficient evidence to go ahead with an indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show me where in your declaration you make reference to this state of urgency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't really know. I'd have to have a look at this. I would have to have a French translation of this, but I just -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Why are you asking him that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I did not hear you. Sorry. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What is the relevance of that question? .

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The Rule 40 measures taken by the Prosecutor was supported by this declaration of the -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That might not be the only document in support of that declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That is correct. I believe he said there was some mention of the urgency in his declaration. I was wondering where it was. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The Rule is very clear on the basis on which the application can be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, in early March 1996 did you know where Mr. Delalic lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: February 1996? I think we had had some information on the basis of which we thought -- well, we were hesitating between Germany and Austria at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And eventually you discovered he was living where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, we discovered that he was living in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your investigation show that Mr. Delalic was registered as a foreigner in Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in the arrest in Germany, so I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my question wasn't about his arrest. My question was did your investigations tell you that Mr. Delalic was registered as a foreigner in Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if that was something that was covered in our investigation, whether he was registered there properly or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to your knowledge you were not informed that he was registered as a foreigner in Germany. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He didn't say that. He says he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know whether he was correctly registered in Germany or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether someone else investigated that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At no time yourself, even after or prior to his arrest, you yourself never verified whether he was registered as a foreigner? Is it correct to say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not quite. We did try to check to see if he was in Germany. Let me repeat, though, I don't know at all whether he was properly registered in Germany or not. We just wanted to see whether he was in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying there was no search done to see whether he was registered? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there's some terms -- register? What do you mean? Do you mean abiding with German legislation? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is correct. A German citizen, a person in Germany, a foreigner or not, is registered in the city in which they live, in the federal state capital. Was this search conducted as to Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to object as to asked and answered and relevancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has said yes or no or and now he's not sure. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think it is consistent that he didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No one ever informed you that he was or was not registered; is that correct? None of your investigators told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall that specific detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the help of the usher I would like to show Mr. Abribat a document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I renew my objection as to relevancy, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Do you know what the document is all about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I have a pretty good idea. You're right, your Honour. Maybe I'll wait and see it and then object. May the Prosecution see the document? (Handed.) Your Honour, the Prosecution objects on relevancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe it is a document previously shown to another witness about specific information about whether or not the accused was or was not registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: May I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is this a document prepared by the witness himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It is addressed to him. Sir, you see that document in front of you, dated 6th March 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's from Sabine Manke to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've seen this document before, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me have a look at it and then I can tell you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually, are you trying to refresh his memory or you think --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I am trying to refresh his memory. Perhaps to save some time, sir, I'm looking at the first paragraph, down four lines, the last word in that line. I'll read it to you. It says: "Delalic, however, was never entered in German central registry of foreign citizens in February 1996". Is there some reason why you would disregard the memos from Sabine Manke?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What is the objection? Actually what is the question, that he disregarded the --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. You have seen this memo before. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That he disregarded the memo. Did he?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That is what I am asking him, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You have concluded. You asked if there was any reason why he disregarded. That's a conclusion that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Did you see and disregard this memo from Sabine Manke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember this memo in particular, but the fourth sentence you have referred to, "Mr. Delalic has not been registered in Germany", that's what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And what is the oversight? What's ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you whether you knew whether he was registered or not, you said you did not know or you couldn't recall. I'm asking you here whether you have seen this memo before and read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe that has been asked and answered. With respect to both questions the witness has said he's not sure. He doesn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You don't know whether you've ever seen this before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Sir, while you were the head of investigations was it the policy of the OTP to have investigators present during arrest procedures and in particular in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Mucic and Delalic's arrest was a first for this Tribunal, so you can't say that there was any procedural what have you, but we had asked to be allowed to be present at the place of arrest, yes, because this is something that is quite common in all countries throughout the world when the police ask for judicial cooperation from the authorities of another country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again with regard to Celebici, was it the Tribunal's policy to provide written translations of indictments and arrest warrants to the accused persons?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry. I don't understand the question. Is the question did this happen in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In Celebici was it your policy to provide written translations of indictments and arrest warrants to the accused persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I will object because I believe it has already been established that at this time there had been no indictment. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: There were no accused persons in Celebici, were there? They were all suspects at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In regards to arrest warrants then, was it your policy to provide written translations of arrest warrants?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must object to that. I believe the record reflects that there was no arrest warrant issued by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. My final question for you, sir: is it correct there was no country seeking the extradition of Mr. Delalic, only this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honours. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. Yes, it's up to you, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Cross-examination by Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Tom Moran and I represent Hazim Delic in this case. I understand you are Divisional Superintendent with the French police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your correct title is Superintendent so I use your correct title. Is that fair enough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Superintendent, you have been a police officer for about 20 years; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that 20 years you've testified a lot of times, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've testified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not unfamiliar with the process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm involved in this kind of proceedings. The proceedings events are totally different so it's fair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to be fair with you, if I ask you a question and you don't understand it, will you stop me and I'll rephrase it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll make a deal with you. I'll try to ask you a direct question. Will you try to give me a direct answer? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Do you want us to be parties to that deal too?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can put my amicus curiae hat on too, if I can make the same deal with the court. Can we have that deal, Superintendent and include the court in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'll answer all of your questions as best I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a direct manner. Some of them may just call for a "yes" or "no." Can you just answer a "yes" or "no" yes with a "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in so far as the question is clear, I'll answer by "yes" and by "no", yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it's not clear, you will stop me and ask me to rephrase it, won't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me start off with this. On I believe it was Professor O'Sullivan's cross-examination you were talking about the military structure in Bosnian Herzegovina, the BH army in 1992 -- 1991/92 time frame. You said there was no rank structure, only functions. What did you mean by that? Did you mean -- let me give you an example. Okay? At one point in my life I was an army officer and I had a rank. I wore it on my shoulders. I also had a function, a job assignment. Was what you mean that someone may have that job assignment but no rank to go with it? Is that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I was trying to say was there wasn't a hierarchy in the Bosnian Army at the time like there wasn't lieutenant, captain, general, etc, but there were people who had command positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm getting at. Someone may be the Commander of a unit -- pick a unit title, anything -- and yet he may not be called captain, lieutenant, colonel or sergeant. Is that what your testimony was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were called "commander".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So that was the only title there was in the Bosnian Army at the time, commander; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you shouldn't really talk about rank rather; just a title, as it were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That was the only military title in the Bosnia-Herzegovina army at the time we are talking about, commander; is that right, is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Let's go on to another subject. Let me talk to you a little bit about your investigation. Because you're the chief investigator for the Tribunal as it applied to this case, you're familiar with the investigation, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I'm familiar with the investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it true that the investigation was difficult because of the reluctance of the parties to cooperate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. We didn't receive any cooperation and we didn't get the cooperation we would have desired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at some point in this investigation some non-government organisations, NGOs, started aiding your investigation, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, taking it in chronological order, it's more us who worked on the basis of reports drawn up by international organisations or NGOs and on the basis of those reports we tried to verify the facts that were written here. The first report that we used was the Maisiski report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the associations you dealt with as the Association of Detainees in Belgrade, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly the title, but if that's what's written down there, no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What the Association of Detainees in Belgrade did was provide written statements from witnesses, perhaps people that were in the Celebici camp, in English, signed by the witness, and sent them to you or some other representative of the Office of the Prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the origin of the first statements, I'm not sure that they were from that association, but the principle was that we'd received all sorts of information referring to testimony or specific acts in respect of which people had testified for whatever organisation. On that basis we tried to get in direct contact with these people to hear their testimony and would have only used testimony that we heard ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you got from somebody in Belgrade statements from witnesses, and those statements had the witnesses' signature on the bottom of them; is that right? Let's start with that. Let's take it one step at a time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't from Belgrade that we obtained the first testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an association which is not in Belgrade, but for security reasons I don't know if I'm authorised to say what it was, the name -- to say what its name was, but it was not in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, from some place. The information you got included statements from witnesses in writing with their signatures on the bottom; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure. I synthesised the information that we had. I began with information which, as I said, was found in the Maisiski report. From that I tried to contact people who could put us in contact with the victims and witnesses. Whether we received copies of testimony from these people there can be no doubt but that was not the basis of our investigating work, which consisted of identifying the victims and witnesses, to try to meet with them and then to take testimony from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's try it again, Superintendent. Did you or other representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor get from someone outside of the Office of the Prosecutor testimonies, statements, whatever of various witnesses prior to the time you interviewed those witnesses? Now I think that calls for a "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we must have received testimonies, yes, but I do not know specifically from what people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it did happen; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That the Tribunal received a great deal of documents, including testimonies, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you that there were about 50 or 60 people on the Prosecution witness list who were somehow connected directly with the Celebici camp, you wouldn't dispute that, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The total number of people that we met with and spoke to was much greater, of course, but that depended on the conditions and the will of the people to testify or lack of will to testify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Some of these people -- let me try it this way: if I were to read out some random names from the Prosecution witness list in a private session and essentially just random, would you remember whether or not you'd gotten testimonies, as you call it, or statements from those witnesses from another source other than your own investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. To that I can answer no, because my work method was to meet with the people. I wanted to find out identities. From that point onwards I could take the statements. I could try to give you the names, but that's not the way I worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So on at least some of these people you talked to before you went and talked to them, you had something in writing from them about what they were going to talk about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Perhaps the Tribunal did have testimonies, but I myself, I always refused to have testimonies before I met the people. What I wanted was to find out their identity and to go to a place where I could question them and then take the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to testifying today, did you talk to anyone in the Office of the Prosecutor about what you were going to testify to, and let me narrow that down just a little bit; okay? Did you know that either late Friday or early today the Prosecution filed a Prosecution response to Mucic defence motion to exclude evidence? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you provide any facts to anyone on the staff of the Office of the Prosecutor in the last two or three weeks about the background of Mr. Mucic's arrest, that kind of thing?
