utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all. I don't remember it, not at all. Over the past three weeks, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You are familiar with the statement that Mr. Mucic gave the Office of the Prosecutor, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just because this came up with a prior witness maybe I might suggest for clarification that the defence counsel ask whether or not anyone from the Office of the Prosecutor had asked him any questions about it. I think there might be some confusion and so later on there's no confusion or accusations, maybe I could ask defence counsel to clarify the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I will ask that question at the request of the Prosecutor, but I would kind of like to do my own cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It's entirely up to the defence. I'm sorry if I was giving unsolicited advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You talked to someone from the Prosecution before you have testified today, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In so far as I was asked to testify, that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. You went over your testimony with someone from the Office of the Prosecutor, the testimony you were going to give today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was merely asked to come testify and I was explained that my testimony had become necessary, because there were changes, but I don't remember what kind. I don't -- I have not been following this trial at all since I left the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So since you arrived back -- when did you arrive in The Hague? Today or yesterday or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yesterday evening at 11 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you didn't talk to, say, Ms McHenry or any of the prosecutors about what you were going to testify to today? You just walked over to the Tribunal, went through the security guards and sat down on the witness stand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not as simple as that, not even to get into this Tribunal, but I did meet with Ms. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you went over your testimony with Miss McHenry before you got on here. That is all I'm trying to get. Nothing wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have to be clear here. We have to understand one another. I did not review my testimony. I was simply told: "You're going to testify. It's going to take place under these conditions", but no details of the testimony were given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So she didn't sit there and say: "I'm going to ask you something along these lines and what would be the answer to that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell me what my answer would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that but she didn't say something like: "What would be your answer be to that question?", or something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, she merely told me that I would be asked a certain number of questions including by herself and then by the defence attorneys and that I should try to remember all the different elements of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. You are familiar with Pavo Mucic's statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember what I took. It was the first, the first. Later on not so much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It kind of stuck in your mind because it was the first one of these statements from a defendant that you'd taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. No. No. No. It didn't remain there in my mind. I have taken hundreds of statements in my professional life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that and in 20 years as a police investigator you have taken more statements than you probably care to remember, but what I want to get at is this: my client's name is mentioned all over that statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I must have referred to his status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. Would it be possible to go through that statement with, say, a black marker and cross out every place my client -- every reference to my client?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I'm not sure what it is you're asking here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking if you could edit that statement in such a way to remove all references to Hazim Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: References to Hazim Delic in Mr. Mucic's statement? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you edit them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frankly I don't think that I had -- in the statement that I took from Mr.. statement (sic) I had no occasion to speak about Hazim Delic and I didn't have time to. I if I did speak about him or mention his name, I don't think I have could have done that very much because I had to leave Vienna after the first interview and unfortunately I was far from having asked him all the questions I could have asked him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try it again, Superintendent. Would it be possible to take some kind of a black marker or something and edit out of that statement in that notebook sitting next to you -- and edit out all references to Hazim Delic? . That is a "yes" or a "no".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Yes" or "no", as you say. If it involves only the part that I participated in in the hearing, that is one-quarter or one-fifth of the total statement, in my opinion you are not going to find many references to Mr. Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try it one more time, Superintendent. Is it possible to go through that statement, Pavo Mucic's statement that is sitting in that -- transcript sitting in that notebook right next to your left elbow and edit out all references to Hazim Delic, and if there aren't any, you don't edit any of them out and if there are a whole lot of them -- can you do that? Is it physically possible to do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose physically it's possible to do it if there are any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of other quick questions and then I think we're done. I don't -- do you have any specialised training in the law beyond that given to police officers? Are you a lawyer? That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a degree in civil law from the University of Bordeaux. Then I studied at the National School for Police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are admitted to practice law if the Republic of France. If you decided you didn't want to be a police officer tomorrow, you could be a lawyer, God for bid. We've got enough lawyers already, judge. Too many of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is plenty of room for more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It's awful tough out there where I come from. You could practice law tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In France in principle advanced studies at the university allow you to go through competitions. I had the proper level for a Magistrates' position, but then as the career would go forth, it would be very different from that of a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand but what I'm getting at is if you retired from the police department tomorrow you could go into the private practice of law. You could get a licence to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have the proper diplomas in order to take the competitions, but not because you have this diploma -- that does not mean you can enter the profession in France. There are rules governing them. You have to meet certain requirements in examinations, specifically specialised training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Thank you very much. Your Honour, I pass the witness. Thank you very much. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. Mr. Ackerman, I think you want to start now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a comment and announcement. During the cross-examination conducted by Mr. Moran Ms. McHenry rose to make a suggestion. It is my position, and I think I have stated it before, that if during a cross-examination of a Prosecution witness it becomes clear to the Prosecutor either that the witness is not being truthful or that the witness has misunderstood the question in such a way that someone is being misled, that it is their obligation to bring that to the attention of the court and counsel. I would not like her to be disabused of that notion by Mr. Moran's remarks, and that I still consider that to be a prosecutorial obligation. The announcement is that I have no questions. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. That's excellent. I think you must have taken the hint, if I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No questions for this witness in re-examination. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think that concludes this witness' examination. He is accordingly discharged. (Witness withdrew from court). JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not think it will be necessary to take any other witness today. So we will have to rise, but before we do, Mr. Greaves had an ex parte motion which we decided this morning. We hope to give a considered ruling about it in due course. It will not be a long time. We will try and give the position of the Trial Chamber on what we said. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am assuming from what was told to us on Friday that the Prosecution's next witness is MR. d'Hooge. Is that still the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct. He will testify about the circumstances with respect to Mr. Mucic, Mr. Delic and Mr. Landzo's statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was my understanding. Thank you. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I would ask if the Prosecutor could, if not today, then tomorrow morning tell us which other witnesses they intend to call, because as things stand the two witnesses may be through tomorrow, and we don't know who will be called next. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I thought that was the last thing that was just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If it will assist, I thought Mr. -- I believe Mr. Ostberg had said this Friday, but just so that there's no confusion, it's the Prosecution's intention after Mr. d'Hooge on Wednesday morning to have Captain Gschwendt -- excuse my pronounciation -- of the Austrian police and after him Mr. Moerbauer, also of the Austrian police. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is the list of witnesses you are expecting within the week. The Trial Chamber will now rise. (5.25 pm)
